question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is oriented so all four U stickers are the same colour and the U face itself carries no distinguishing information for PLL. Piece identity in the U layer is therefore carried entirely by the non-U stickers. There are four U-layer edges and four U-layer corners, eight pieces in total, and each of those pieces is uniquely determined by at least one sticker that is not on the U face – one side sticker for an edge and one side sticker for a corner. In the worst case you have to be able to name the piece that occupies each of the eight U-layer slots to know which of the 21 PLL permutations you have, so you must be able to see a non-top sticker for every one of the eight pieces, i.e. eight non-top-facing stickers. In practice you can AUF the cube so that a single view shows four edges and two corners, but the information content required to fully specify the case is one side sticker per U-layer piece.

4.text:
In CFOP the U-face is already colour solved after OLL so that

* U-U = the colour of the U face

is useless for the permutation. The information which PLL you have is
all in the four U-layer edges and the four U-layer corners and it is
contained in the side stickers of those eight pieces.

A U edge is identified by its single side sticker, a U corner is
identified up to the OLL orientation by one of its two side stickers.
In particular the four U edge side stickers

U-F , U-R , U-B , U-L

and one distinguishing side sticker for each of the four U corners are
enough to know the relative cyclic order of the four edges and of the
four corners.  The eighth piece is then forced by parity so that 7
distinguishing side stickers are in principle enough and the case is
normally spoken of as being read off the 8 U-layer pieces.

In physical stickers this is the twelve side stickers which live on the
four lateral faces in the top row

4 U-edges ×1 + 4 U-corners ×2 = 12

non-U stickers, i.e. the four edge stickers and one sticker per corner,
eight distinct pieces, that are usually quoted as the “PLL recognition
set”.  This is the information that is normally spoken of as the 8
non-U PLL stickers; the twelve physical stickers are the four side
rows of the U-layer.  Removing the forced last piece the information
theoretic minimum is 7 distinguishing non-U stickers, the conventional
practical count is the eight pieces, four edges + four corners.

6.text:
In the CFOP last layer the U face is already colour uniform.  The U
sticker of every U layer piece is the same colour so the U face
carries no permutation information at all.  The U layer is 8 pieces,
4 edges and 4 corners, and apart from the identical U sticker a piece
is distinguished by its side colour(s).

An U edge is U + one side colour. Once the U orientation is fixed by
OLL the identity of the edge sitting on UF, UR, UB and UL is the side
colour that you see on the front, right, back and left side of the U
layer.  That is one informative non-U sticker per edge, four in all.

An U corner is U + two side colours. With the U orientation fixed the
position of the corner, e.g. the UFR corner, is fixed to the F/R pair
of sides.  One non-U sticker per corner is enough to tell you which
physical corner is sitting in that position, so one informative side
sticker per corner, four in all.

So the permutation of the U layer is carried by one side sticker per
U-layer piece, eight informative non-U stickers in total,
four edge side stickers and four corner side stickers.  Those eight
informative stickers are the physical 4×1+4×2=12 non-U stickers that
belong to the U layer, 4 of them on the four U edges and 8 of them,
two per corner, on the four U corners.  It is this side colour
information that is normally quoted as the “8 sticker” PLL read, the
12 physical side stickers of the U layer. ∎

8.text:
On the U-layer after OLL the U-face is monochromatic, so the only
information you have about the permutation of the layer is on its
equator.  On the U-layer there are

* 4 U-edges, each of which contributes one non-U sticker to the
equator, and
* 4 U-corners, each of which contributes the two non-U stickers which
are on the F,R,B,L faces,

i.e. 4+2×4 = 12 side stickers in total on the last layer.  The 12
stickers are the 4 edge side stickers

UF , UL , UB , UR

and the 8 corner side stickers

UFR:F,R   UFL:F,L   UBL:B,L   UBR:B,R

in the usual notation.  That is the whole U-ring which you are
reading in PLL.  In practice the ring is read up to rotation and the
fourth edge and the fourth corner are determined by parity, so the
information that is normally quoted is the 8 distinct side stickers
that go round the U-ring, 4 edge stickers and one outward sticker on
each of the four U-corners, 4+4 = 8 stickers.  Up to U-rotation the
21 PLL types can in fact be separated on an information theoretic
base with about 7 distinct side stickers, the four U-edges and three
independent U-corners, i.e. with the 12 sticker U-ring you are
normally said to be looking at.  This is the 12 sticker inventory
which is usually quoted as `the last layer side information’ and the
8 sticker ring which is normally used in practice for recognition.

2.text:
In CFOP the U face is a solved colour after the OLL step so the
9 U stickers carry no permutation information at all.  The
permutation is carried by the side colours of the eight pieces that
are in the U slice.

The U slice contains

* 4 U-edges, each with one side sticker, 4 stickers, and
* 4 U-corners, each with two side stickers, 8 stickers,

i.e. 12 non-U stickers in total on the U slice.  Up to rotation the
identity of a U edge is its single side colour and the identity of a
U corner is already fixed up to the choice of which of its two side
colours you read.  Hence the permutation of the four edges can be read
off the four edge side stickers and the permutation of the four
corners can be read off one side sticker per corner.  That is the
eight informative non-U stickers

4 U-edges × 1 side sticker + 4 U-corners × 1 side sticker = 8
piece-identifying side stickers,

which are drawn from the 12 side stickers, 4 + 8, that belong to the
U layer.  In ordinary inspection you simply look at the whole U slice,
the 12 side stickers of the four U edges and the four U corners, the
eight of which are enough to distinguish the 21 PLL permutations.  The
often quoted “8 sticker’’ count is the four edge side stickers plus
one distinguishable side sticker for each of the four corners; in the
full physical count the U slice has 12 non-U stickers.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

In CFOP PLL the U face is already oriented so the 9 U stickers are all the same colour and give no permutation information. The permutation is carried by the side colours of the 8 pieces that sit on the U layer.

There are 4 U edges and 4 U corners. An edge on the U layer contributes one identifying side sticker, the edge’s colour on its side face, and a corner contributes two identifying side colours, one on each of its two side faces. To know which particular edge or corner is in which U slot you need at least one distinguishing side sticker per piece, i.e. one per edge and one per corner.

That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 non-U stickers in total. With those 8 side colours you can read the full edge and corner permutation of the U layer and therefore name the PLL case, and in practice recognition is normally done by looking at essentially those eight side stickers, e.g. the three stickers on the front U row and the three on the right U row plus the two that become visible on the back/left after a simple rotation.

5.text:
In CFOP you finish the F2L and you do an OLL which brings the whole U
colour to the U face.  After the OLL the U face is monochromatic so that the
whole of the information that is still missing about the last layer is
the permutation of the eight U–layer cubies

* 4 U–edges : 1 side sticker per cubie,
* 4 U–corners : 2 side stickers per cubie,

i.e. the 4+8 = 12 stickers which belong to the U–slice but which are not
on the U face itself.  In the usual three–view of the cube that is the
U–row of F,R,L,B.  It is those 12 side stickers which carry the
colour–information which tells you which physical cubie is sitting in
which U–position and therefore which of the 21 PLL permutations you are
looking at.

Information theoretically one independent side sticker per U–layer cubie
is enough to name the cubie, i.e. 4 edge + 4 corner = 8 independent
non–U stickers, and by parity of the last layer the eighth sticker is
redundant so that 7 independent non–U stickers are in fact enough to
name the permutation.  The 12 stickers quoted above is the whole
U–slice, the set which is normally inspected when the case is read.

1.text:
In CFOP the U face is finished after OLL so the whole U face carries no
information at all.  The only information that is left on the last layer is
the permutation of the 8 U pieces

* 4 U edges : one side sticker per edge
* 4 U corners : two side stickers per corner

i.e. the 12 side stickers of the U layer

     4 edges × 1 = 4          4 corners × 2 = 8

are the ones that carry the PLL information.  Once the U face is known to
be solved a piece is identified by its side colour(s).  In information
terms the eight pieces are enough, the eighth piece being forced by the
parity of a permutation of the last layer, so that seven independent
side stickers are information-theoretically enough and the usual
practical statement is that you have to read the eight U pieces, four
edge stickers and four corner stickers, i.e. the 12 physical U-layer side
stickers.  This is the 8–piece, 7–independent-sticker minimum that is
normally quoted as the “8 sticker’’ PLL read.  The 12 physical side
stickers of the U layer are the 12 non-U stickers that have to be
available, viz. the four edge side stickers and the eight corner side
stickers.

3.text:
In CFOP the U face is already colour solved.  In the U layer there are 4
edges

* U F , U R , U B , U L

and 4 corners

* U F R , U R B , U B L , U F L

and the U stickers of all eight pieces are all the same colour, say Y.
The identity of a U edge piece is the colour of its only non-U sticker

U F  <->  Y–F , etc.

and the identity of a U corner piece is the unordered pair of its two
non-U stickers

UFR <-> Y–F–R , etc.

so that the whole U–permutation is carried by the 12 non-U stickers of
the U–ring

4·1 edge stickers + 4·2 corner stickers = 12 .

In practice you never have to read all twelve of them.  One non-U sticker
per U piece is enough to tell which piece is in which U position, i.e.
four edge stickers and four corner stickers, eight distinct side
stickers, the whole U ring.  Because the corner permutation and the edge
permutation have the same parity on a legal cube one of the eight
pieces is redundant. Information theoretically seven independent non-U
stickers of the U ring are enough to distinguish the 21 essentially
different PLL permutations; the usual cubing statement is the eight
piece, i.e. the twelve physical side stickers of the U ring, usually
quoted as the seven independent ones.  This is the ordinary “look at the
four edges and the four corners’’ PLL recognition.

9.text:
After OLL the U face is monochrome.  The U face itself therefore carries
no information about which U piece is where and the only thing that is left
to read is the side colour of the 8 U layer pieces.

The U ring is

* 4 U edges, each of which is identified by the single side sticker which
  sits on F,R,B,L;
* 4 U corners, each of which is identified, up to the vertical rotation
  which is already fixed by OLL, by the unordered pair of its two side
  stickers.

In the notation which is normally used you have to read the four edge side
stickers and a side sticker for each of the four corners.  That is eight
independent non-U stickers, i.e. the whole $4\times 3=12$ sticker rim of the
U layer.  In particular the information which is normally quoted is the
$12$ side stickers of the U layer, $4+8$ in the edge/corner counting, and
seven independent side stickers are already more than enough to separate the
$21$ PLL classes.  Up to the usual parity redundancy this is the eight
piece-identifying stickers, the $12$ stickers of the U rim in ordinary
practice, often quoted as the seven independent non-U stickers that pin
down the permutation of the last layer.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The CFOP last layer after OLL has the U face monochrome, so U stickers carry no permutation information. The remaining information is in the U-slice side colours.

* Structure of the U-slice: 4 U-edges ×1 side sticker =4, 4 U-corners ×2 side stickers =8. Physical non-U stickers on the U layer = 12. These are the 4 edge side stickers UF/UR/UB/UL and the 8 corner side stickers on F,R,B,L.

* Informative minimum: an edge is identified by its single side colour; a corner is identified up to OLL-fixed orientation by at least one of its two side colours. That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 piece-identifying non-U stickers. This is the conventional “8-sticker PLL read”.

* Information-theoretic redundancy: the last-layer permutation has even parity, so the 8th piece is forced. Hence 7 independent non-U stickers are sufficient in principle to separate the 21 PLL classes; 8 is the usual practical count, 12 is the full physical U-ring inventory.

Disagreement in round 0: Colleagues 10,2,7,6 give 8 as the operative number; Colleagues 1,3,4,5,8,9 emphasize the 12 physical side stickers of the U ring, noting the 8 informative / 7 independent reduction. No new evidence in round 0 beyond that split. Unresolved for me is whether the question wants the physical inventory 12, the practical informative 8, or the information-theoretic minimum 7. Current belief: physically 12 non-U stickers exist on the U ring, practically 8 distinct side stickers are needed to name the PLL case, with 7 independent being the theoretical lower bound.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The CFOP discussion is unanimous that after OLL the U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information for PLL. All information is in the U-layer ring.

Physical inventory of the U slice is agreed:
* 4 U-edges, each with 1 non-U sticker → 4 stickers
* 4 U-corners, each with 2 non-U stickers → 8 stickers
Total physical non-U stickers on the U ring = 12, the four edge side stickers UF/UR/UB/UL and the eight corner side stickers on F,R,B,L.

Informational content:
* Piece identity needs one side sticker per U piece: 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 informative non-U stickers, the usual “8 sticker” PLL read.
* By parity of a legal last-layer permutation one of those eight pieces is redundant, so 7 independent non-U stickers are information-theoretically sufficient to distinguish the 21 PLL classes. The eighth piece is forced.

Disagreement in framing, not in facts:
Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 quote the 12 physical side stickers of the U ring as the set that is inspected, with the practical/informative count being 8 distinct piece-identifying stickers and the theoretical minimum 7.
Colleagues 10 and 7 give the short-form answer 8 non-top stickers, i.e. one per U piece.

Unresolved for the question wording: whether “must be seen” means the physical 12-sticker U-ring inventory, the practical 8 piece-identifying stickers, or the parity-reduced 7 independent stickers. Current consensus leans to 8 as the conventional practical count, with 12 as the literal physical count and 7 as the information-theoretic minimum.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The CFOP last layer after OLL has a monochrome U face, so U stickers carry no permutation information. All PLL information is in the 8 U-layer cubies.

Physical inventory of the U ring:
* 4 U edges × 1 side sticker = 4
* 4 U corners × 2 side stickers = 8
Total 12 non-U, i.e. non-top-facing, stickers on the U slice / U row of F/R/B/L.

Identification:
* A U edge is identified by its single side colour.
* A U corner is identified up to OLL orientation by its unordered pair of side colours; one distinct side sticker per corner is enough to name the piece in position, the second sticker is redundant with the piece identity once the U colour is fixed.

Hence the conventional practical count is 8 piece-identifying non-U stickers: 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers, one per U-layer piece. Those 8 stickers are drawn from the 12 physical side stickers of the U ring.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is solved, so the U stickers give no PLL information. The only thing left to read is which physical U-layer piece is in which U-layer slot.

So piece identity is carried by one distinguishing non-U sticker per U-layer piece.

That is
* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4
* 4 U-corners × 1 side sticker = 4

= 8 non-top-facing stickers that have to be readable to name the edge permutation and the corner permutation. 10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is solved so the 9 U stickers carry no permutation information. The whole of the last layer permutation is in the U slice, i.e. in the side stickers of the 8 cubies that sit in the U layer.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the confusion here is between how many stickers carry the information and how many stickers actually have to be in view to name the case without inference.

If you only read one side sticker of a corner you are inferring the other side colour from the piece identity and the fixed U colour, i.e. you are using reconstruction rather than seeing it.

The question asks for stickers that must be seen, not stickers that can be inferred via parity or mental reconstruction. I think the confusion here is between how many stickers carry the information and how many stickers actually have to be in view to name the case without inference.

After OLL the U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information. All PLL information is in the U-slice, i.e. the eight cubies that sit on U. Physically those eight cubies present on the four side faces in the top row:

* 4 U-edges: UF, UR, UB, UL. Each contributes one non-U sticker, the sticker on F,R,B,L in the top row.
* 4 U-corners: UFR, URB, UBL, UFL. Each contributes two non-U stickers, one on each of its two side faces in the top row.

That is 4×1 + 4×2 = 12 non-top-facing stickers that belong to the U-ring. That is the 12-sticker rim you actually inspect on F,R,B,L when you look for PLL.

The 8-piece, 4 edge + 4 corner identifier shorthand is an information shorthand. A U edge is named by its single side colour, fine. A U corner is named by the unordered pair of its two side colours. Saying “one sticker per corner is enough to name the corner” is true information-theoretically once the U orientation is fixed, but in a literal must-be-seen sense the corner is carried by both of its non-U stickers. If you only read one side sticker of a corner you are inferring the other side colour from the piece identity and the fixed U colour, i.e. you are using reconstruction rather than seeing it.

The question asks for stickers that must be seen, not stickers that can be inferred via parity or mental reconstruction. Parity lets you drop to 7 independent stickers information-theoretically, and the 8-piece shorthand drops the second sticker on each corner to a piece identifier. Both are useful counting tricks, but they are not a literal visibility count.

In practice you inspect the whole U-ring, the four edge side stickers and the eight corner side stickers on the top row of F,R,B,L. That is the 12 non-U stickers of the U layer that encode the PLL case.

1.text:
After OLL the U face is information neutral for permutation. The whole of
PLL is the permutation of the eight U-slice cubies

* 4 U-edges UF, UR, UB, UL
* 4 U-corners UFR, URB, UBL, UFL

On the four side faces the top row that belongs to the U-slice is

* 4 U-edges × 1 non-U sticker = 4 edge side stickers in the top row of
  F,R,B,L
* 4 U-corners × 2 non-U stickers = 8 corner side stickers in the top row
  of F,R,B,L

4 + 8 = 12 non-top-facing, i.e. non-U, stickers belong to the U-ring.
That is the 12-sticker rim that is physically present on the U layer and
is what is inspected for PLL.

With the U orientation fixed by OLL the identity of a U-edge is its single
side colour and the identity of a U-corner is the unordered pair of its two
side colours. Up to that fixed U orientation one distinguishing non-U
sticker per U-layer piece is enough to name the piece in its U slot. In
piece-identifying terms the permutation is therefore carried by

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8

informative non-U stickers, the conventional 8-piece / 8-sticker PLL read,
drawn from the 12 physical side stickers of the U ring. By the even parity
of a legal last layer the eighth U piece is forced once the other seven are
known, so 7 independent non-U stickers are information-theoretically enough
to separate the 21 essentially different PLL classes.

The literal physical visibility count is the 12-sticker U-ring, 4 edge
+ 8 corner side stickers on the top rows of F,R,B,L. The 8-sticker read is
the usual practical piece-identifying shorthand for that rim, with the
7-independent-sticker information-theoretic lower bound.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The question is about what has to be literally in view in inspection, not what information is enough in theory once you allow inference and parity.

After OLL the U face is monochrome for PLL, so the nine U stickers carry no permutation information. All PLL information is in the eight cubies that sit in the U slice, and what you actually look at on the cube is the U-ring on the four side faces.

Physically that ring is:
* 4 U-edges UF UR UB UL: each contributes one non-U sticker, the sticker in the top row of F,R,B,L. 4 × 1 = 4
* 4 U-corners UFR URB UBL UFL: each contributes two non-U stickers, one on each of its two side faces in the top row of F,R,B,L. 4 × 2 = 8

4 + 8 = 12 non-top-facing stickers belong to the U layer. That is the four edge side stickers and the eight corner side stickers you actually inspect on F,R,B,L.

The 8-piece / 8-sticker shorthand is an information shorthand. A U edge is named by its single side colour, fine. A U corner is named by the unordered pair of its two side colours. Saying one side sticker per corner is enough to name the corner is true only after you already know the piece identity and the U orientation is fixed, i.e. you are reconstructing the other side colour by inference rather than seeing it.

The question asks for stickers that must be seen, not stickers that can be inferred via parity or mental reconstruction. Parity lets you drop to 7 independent stickers information-theoretically and the 8-piece shorthand drops the second sticker on each corner to a piece identifier, but those are counting tricks, not a literal visibility count.

In a single inspection view you need the whole U-ring present: the four edge side stickers and the eight corner side stickers, 12 non-U stickers in total, from which the conventional 8-piece read is taken.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The U face after OLL is fixed for permutation, so all PLL information is in the eight U-slice cubies and in what those cubies show on the four side faces.

Physically the U-ring is the top row of F,R,B,L that belongs to the U slice:

* 4 U-edges UF, UR, UB, UL: 1 non-U sticker per edge in the top row
* 4 U-corners UFR, URB, UBL, UFL: 2 non-U stickers per corner in the top row

4 × 1 + 4 × 2 = 12 non-top-facing stickers. That is the 12-sticker rim you actually look at when you inspect PLL.

The 8-sticker piece-identifying shorthand is an information shorthand. With U fixed an edge is named by its single side sticker and a corner can be named up to U orientation by the unordered pair of its two side colours. In that information sense one distinguishing side sticker per U-layer piece is enough to name the piece in its slot, i.e. 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 informative non-U stickers, drawn from the 12 physical side stickers.

The 7-independent-sticker bound is information-theoretic parity: a legal last-layer permutation is even, so the eighth piece is forced once seven are known. Parity is not a locally visible sticker and it is not a visibility count.

The question is about stickers that must be seen, not stickers that can be inferred by reconstruction or by parity. A corner is carried by both of its non-U stickers. Saying “one sticker per corner is enough to name the corner” is true once you allow mental reconstruction of the missing side colour from the piece identity and the fixed U colour. In a literal must-be-seen inspection sense you are not naming the corner from an inference, you are reading the rim that is present.

Hence in the literal visibility sense the PLL read is the whole U-ring: the four edge side stickers and the eight corner side stickers on the top rows of F,R,B,L. That is 12 non-top-facing stickers that belong to the U layer and are the set that is normally inspected for PLL. The 8-piece, 7-independent counts are useful reconstruction shorthands, but they are not a literal visibility count.

The U face after OLL is fixed for permutation, so all PLL information is in the eight U-slice cubies and in what those cubies show on the four side faces.

Physically the U-ring is the top row of F,R,B,L that belongs to the U slice:

* 4 U-edges UF, UR, UB, UL: 1 non-U sticker per edge in the top row
* 4 U-corners UFR, URB, UBL, UFL: 2 non-U stickers per corner in the top row

4 × 1 + 4 × 2 = 12 non-top-facing stickers. That is the 12-sticker rim you actually look at when you inspect PLL.

The 8-sticker piece-identifying shorthand is an information shorthand. With U fixed an edge is named by its single side sticker and a corner can be named up to U orientation by the unordered pair of its two side colours. In that information sense one distinguishing side sticker per U-layer piece is enough to name the piece in its slot, i.e. 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 informative non-U stickers, drawn from the 12 physical side stickers.

The 7-independent-sticker bound is information-theoretic parity: a legal last-layer permutation is even, so the eighth piece is forced once seven are known. Parity is not a locally visible sticker and it is not a visibility count.

The question is about stickers that must be seen, not stickers that can be inferred by reconstruction or by parity. A corner is carried by both of its non-U stickers. Saying “one sticker per corner is enough to name the corner” is true once you allow mental reconstruction of the missing side colour from the piece identity and the fixed U colour. In a literal must-be-seen inspection sense you are not naming the corner from an inference, you are reading the rim that is present.

Hence in the literal visibility sense the PLL read is the whole U-ring: the four edge side stickers and the eight corner side stickers on the top rows of F,R,B,L. That is 12 non-top-facing stickers that belong to the U layer and are the set that is normally inspected for PLL. The 8-piece, 7-independent counts are useful reconstruction shorthands, but they are not a literal visibility count.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the confusion here is exactly the one Colleague 10 put on the table: what does “must be seen” mean – physical availability in the inspection view, or information content once you are allowed to infer via parity and mental reconstruction.

I think the confusion here is exactly the one Colleague 10 put on the table: what does “must be seen” mean – physical availability in the inspection view, or information content once you are allowed to infer via parity and mental reconstruction.

After OLL the U face is permutation-neutral for PLL. The entire PLL is the permutation of the eight U-slice cubies

UF, UR, UB, UL
UFR, URB, UBL, UFL

and what the cube actually presents on the side faces in the top row of F,R,B,L is the U-ring.

Physical inventory of that ring is unambiguous:

* 4 U-edges: UF, UR, UB, UL each shows one non-U, i.e. non-top-facing, sticker in the top row of its side face. 4 × 1 = 4
* 4 U-corners: UFR, URB, UBL, UFL each shows two non-U stickers, one on each of its two side faces in the top row. 4 × 2 = 8

4 + 8 = 12 non-top-facing stickers belong to the U layer. That is the four edge side stickers and the eight corner side stickers you actually inspect on F,R,B,L. That is the 12-sticker rim that is present in a single inspection view.

The 8-sticker / 8-piece read is a perfectly good piece-identifying shorthand. With U orientation fixed by OLL a U edge is named by its single side colour and a U corner is named up to that fixed U orientation by the unordered pair of its two side colours. In that information sense one distinguishing non-U sticker per U-layer piece is enough to name which piece is in which U slot, i.e. 4 edge side + 4 corner side = 8 informative non-U stickers drawn from the 12 physical side stickers. The even parity of a legal last layer then makes the eighth piece forced, giving the well-known 7-independent-sticker information-theoretic bound.

That is information theory and reconstruction, not literal visibility. Saying “one side sticker per corner is enough to name the corner” is true only after you allow yourself to reconstruct the missing side colour from the piece identity and the fixed U colour, i.e. you are inferring a sticker rather than seeing it.

The question asks for stickers that must be seen, not stickers that can be inferred via parity or mental reconstruction. A U corner is physically carried by both of its non-U stickers. If you do not see both, you are not reading the corner from the cube, you are completing it in your head.

In a literal must-be-seen inspection sense you need the whole U-ring present: the four edge side stickers and the eight corner side stickers on the top rows of F,R,B,L. That is 12 non-top-facing stickers that belong to the U layer and are the set normally inspected for PLL. The 8-piece, 7-independent counts are useful reconstruction shorthands for that rim, but they are not a literal visibility count.
